5. SimBrief flight

The SimBrief flight tab reads your latest SimBrief plan and only activates the sceneries of that flight's airports; they are removed automatically when you close MSFS.

A typical flight

  1. Prepare your flight on SimBrief: 🌐 Open SimBrief button.
  2. In Hangar FS 2024, enter your SimBrief ID (the first time) and click Fetch the latest flight plan.
  3. The app shows the departure and arrival in large letters, like a ticket, then the route and the airports found (departure, arrival and, if the "Include alternate airports" tile is on, the alternates), with the matching sceneries of your library.
  4. Click ✈ Prepare the flight (link sceneries): only those sceneries are linked in Community.
  5. Click ▶ Launch MSFS 2024. This button only exists in this tab, to start the simulator once the sceneries are ready.
  6. When MSFS closes, the flight's sceneries are removed from Community if the "Remove sceneries automatically when the simulator closes" tile is on, and the plan is cleared. ★ protected add-ons are never removed.

Good to know

  • The flight options are tiles: one click switches a tile on (light and "ON") or off. A green banner under the buttons shows the current flight.
  • ■ End the flight (remove sceneries), the orange button, removes the current flight without waiting for MSFS to close.
  • Several sceneries for the same airport: "Prepare the flight" asks which one to activate (your last choice is suggested). The others are set aside during the flight if they were active, then put back afterwards.
  • Keep some sceneries for every flight: protect them with ★ Protect (button at the bottom of the Library, or right-click the row). ☆ Unprotect removes the star without removing them from Community. They are never removed or set aside by a SimBrief flight.
  • Load only the flight's sceneries: when the tile is on, "Prepare the flight" sets aside the other airport sceneries activated in the Library, then puts them back after the flight. ★ protected add-ons, aircraft, tools and libraries are never touched.
  • A scenery not recognised? Fix its codes with ICAO codes… in the Library.
  • "Stop the relay when the simulator closes" stops the relay when MSFS closes; it restarts with it.

6. Flight plan & tracking

Flight plan & tracking opens the Flight plan page (built into the app) in its own full-screen window, with live tracking of your flight, MSFS AI traffic and the pilots of your FSHub VA online.

Opening and closing: ✈ Flight plan & tracking tab (orange marker in the taskbar). The red ✕ CLOSE button, top right of the page, closes the window. External links (SimBrief, FSHub, radars) open in your usual browser.

The page uses the app's colours: dark cards, sky-blue titles and main button, rounded buttons.

The main page

  • Two columns: the FMS on the left, the destinations on the right. Below the three steps, the 🗺 Pick departure and arrival on the map button opens the Personal flight plan map.
  • FMS: at the top, the mode (Departure → Arrival or Random / duration), then three numbered steps: 1 the aircraft, 2 the departure, 3 the arrival (or the flight duration in random mode). The lit button is the one selected.
  • Options (folded, one click to open): Departures / Arrivals, IFR / VFR, the Time of flight and the cruise altitude. When closed, they show a summary of your choices, for example "IFR · FL370 · any time". The times stay visible right below.
  • Time of flight: Any, Morning, Day, Dusk or Night. In Departure → Arrival, the app shows in UTC the time to set in MSFS, 30 min before takeoff to get ready (1 h for a wide-body or a flight over 4 h), then takeoff and arrival with the light on arrival; the time is computed so the moment fits both airports (Dusk: takeoff in daylight, landing just after sunset) and it is sent to SimBrief. It also shows whether it is day or night right now at your two airports. In Random / duration, you depart now from the airport you chose (it never changes): the app only offers destinations where it will be the right time on landing.
  • Destinations: they match the chosen aircraft (real airports with a suitable runway for an airliner, large airports for a wide-body), with runway compatibility: length, but also width (an airliner is refused under 30 m, "to check" under 45 m; 45 m for a wide-body) and facilities (a field without scheduled commercial flights, small airfield or military base, is marked "to check" for an airliner, cause 🏢 Facilities).
  • Day / night strip: under the flight time, a bar shows whether you fly by day (yellow), at dawn or dusk (orange) or by night (blue), with the local takeoff and landing time of each airport and the UTC time. It follows the aircraft's position from its speed and the sun's movement, seen from cruise altitude (up high you see the sun longer than on the ground); it also announces a sunrise or sunset en route. If the database doesn't know an airfield's runways, it is marked "to check" (orange) instead of being refused.
  • Chosen destination: clicking a destination shows, under the list, a route preview on a small map, the distance, the flight time (from takeoff to landing, climb and descent included, taxi not included) with below it the estimated "gate to gate" block time (flight time + typical taxi: 10 min light aircraft, 20 min turboprop or jet, 30 min wide-body; each destination in the list shows it too), and the Export box, with two separate buttons: SimBrief and .PLN file (clicking SimBrief doesn't download a .PLN). Until a destination is chosen, a short sentence takes their place.

The Personal flight plan map (🗺 Pick departure and arrival on the map button of the Flight plan page): the full-screen map where you click a departure then an arrival. It always opens empty, with no airport selected, so you are completely free, and shows the night area live (dark blue veil, dawn and dusk shaded, orange sunrise / sunset line, UTC time at the bottom left). The top bar is arranged on two rows. Top: Main menu, the route summary (departure → arrival, distance, compatibility), Swap, Clear, Validate and the cross to close. Bottom: Click sets (▲ Departure and ■ Arrival tiles: choose what your next click does; with no choice, the 1st click sets the departure and the 2nd the arrival), the airport filters (Large, Medium; only fields with a real 4-letter ICAO code are shown, and their code shows when you zoom in; small airfields are in the VFR plan page), the aircraft, the altitude and Dark background. The Map background button changes the background (Map, Dark map, Satellite, Terrain). A legend, bottom right, recalls the colours and folds with a click on its title. Grey circles with a red dashed outline are airports incompatible with your aircraft (too far or unsuitable runway). Once departure and arrival are chosen, the legend also shows the flight's day / night strip (see Flight plan).

VFR plan (VFR plan menu entry, Prepare section): a page to draw your flight your own way, like on a VFR chart. Click anywhere on the map to add a point, or on an airport, a VOR / DME or an NDB (the point then takes its name, for example TOU; a free point is called WP1, WP2…). To change the order of the points, click a point in the My VFR route list (it is highlighted), then ▲ / ▼ or the up / down arrow keys: only its position changes, the other points stay as they are. Drag a point to move it; to remove it, use ✕ in the right-hand list, or right-click it then Remove from route. Each leg shows its magnetic heading (variation of the nearest beacon) and distance, and the right column lists your points (heading and distance to reach them) with the total distance. VOR / DMEs are white hexagons with a navy border (different from airports) and NDBs are purple circles; if you imported the MSFS navigation data, the NDBs come from there. Small airfields appear from a medium zoom (no need to zoom in very close). The Airports, VOR / DME, NDB, Runway axes (5 NM extended centreline in yellow dashes when zoomed in) and Names buttons turn on or off, and Map background changes the background: Terrain (coloured relief, OpenTopoMap), Topo, Map, Dark map or Satellite. No altitude or fuel to set. The Aircraft choice (single-engine, twin-engine, light turboprops, or any ICAO code typed by hand, e.g. C414) is used for SimBrief and for the flight time: next to the aircraft name, its cruise speed in knots (normal cruise at low altitude, e.g. 115 kt for a C172, 195 kt for a C414). Change it if you fly faster or slower: it is kept for this aircraft. The CRUISE box sets the cruise altitude in feet (3500 ft by default): it is written to the .PLN file, sent to SimBrief and to the FMS. Under the totals, the app checks the terrain under your route (the centreline and 1 NM each side, except 2 NM around the departure and arrival airports): if the cruise altitude does not leave at least 1000 ft above the highest point (2000 ft in mountains, above 3000 ft), the leg turns red in the list and on the map, the peak is marked, and the Climb to … button sets the advised altitude (VFR half-level according to the route direction). A small profile shows the terrain and your altitude. Terrain data comes from the Internet (free elevation tiles): it is an aid, not a guarantee, always check your VFR chart. The right list then shows the time of each leg and the total flight time (from takeoff to landing: the legs plus 5 min of circuit at departure and arrival, no wind), and below it the estimated "gate to gate" block time (+10 min taxi). My routes (right column): give your route a name, then 💾 Save; the list below lets you open it again (Open) or delete it (✕). They are kept in the app's settings folder and stay after an update. 📂 Open a .PLN (top bar) loads an existing plan (yours, Little Navmap's or one from the MSFS world map) so you can change it: the SID, STAR and approaches in the file come back as plain points, to choose again in the airport card if you want. Start and end on an airport, then SimBrief (route point by point, VFR rules) or .PLN file to load in MSFS 2024. Your route is kept when you close the page. Data: OurAirports; Terrain background: © OpenStreetMap, OpenTopoMap.

RNAV, ILS, SID, STAR and approaches (VFR plan page): at the bottom of the right column, Import from MSFS. Do it once, with MSFS 2024 open at the main menu: the app reads from your simulator the RNAV points, VORs, ILSs, NDBs, departures (SID), arrivals (STAR) and approaches of every airport in the world (add-ons included) and keeps them on your PC; a bar shows the progress, allow a few minutes. Then everything works with the simulator off. The RNAV (small blue triangles, when zoomed in) and ILS (green cone along the approach axis, with frequency and course) buttons turn on, and you can click them to make them a point of your route. Right-click an airport (or its ILS) to open its card: runways, ILS (frequency and course), Departures (SID), Arrivals (STAR) and Approaches. When it opens, the map centres on the airport and draws all its procedures, with their name at the end ("show on map" boxes to hide some): you see at a glance where each SID goes and where each STAR comes from. Click a procedure to highlight it, choose its runway and transition, then Choose: the SID is added after your departure airport (orange), the STAR (blue) and the approach (green) before your arrival airport, in the list, the distance and the .PLN file. For each runway direction, the app also adds a visual approach (VISUAL 09, VISUAL 27…), like the MSFS Garmin GPS units: STRGHT 5 NM out on the centreline, FINAL at 2.5 NM (3° path altitude, e.g. 1400 ft for a 558 ft field, and FAF for the FMS) then the runway threshold. It is mostly useful for fields without an instrument approach. The card also lets you set an airport as departure or arrival. Right-clicking a point of your route or a beacon opens its card (Remove, Add to route). SimBrief gets your route with the SID, the STAR and the departure and arrival runways. The VORs and NDBs of your route are sent by their coordinates (otherwise SimBrief could pick a beacon with the same name elsewhere in the world, e.g. TAN taken for Tangier); official 5-letter points without digits (e.g. OSVEG), unique worldwide, are sent by their name, which is more precise. If you chose an approach, it gets the arrival runway but not the approach points: SimBrief and Navigraph link your last point to the start of the approach and add it themselves (on the SimBrief map the line goes straight to the runway, that is normal; in Navigraph, check that the approach and its transition are the ones you chose). Run the import again (Update from MSFS) after a big simulator update.

The flight log

Open it with Flight log in the left menu, or the Flight log button of the tracking map. It fills in by itself during the flight, as long as the Flight plan & tracking window is open.

  • On the left, the timeline: Gate, Pushback, Taxi to runway, Takeoff, Climb, Cruise, Descent, Approach, Landing, Taxi to gate, Arrival gate. The current phase is orange, completed phases blue. Each phase shows its time, duration, fuel on board (with what was burned), taxi speed (average and max) on the ground and indicated airspeed (IAS) in flight, vertical speed and altitude; at takeoff the liftoff speed, on approach the speed and vertical speed on final (passing 500 ft AGL), at landing the touchdown rate (Butter, Soft, Good, Firm, Hard), speed and flaps.
  • At the top, the summary: block time (gate to gate), flight time (takeoff → landing), fuel on board (and burned), distance, max altitude and landing, compared with the SimBrief plan.
  • The flight profile, ground to ground: dashed, the profile planned by SimBrief with TOC (top of climb) and TOD (top of descent); in colour, your actual profile, phase by phase.
  • The map: only your route (SID in green, route in pink, STAR in orange, as on the tracking map) and your track. The ✈ AI traffic button, at the top left of the map below the + and − buttons ("hidden" at first, one click for "shown"), shows the AI aircraft flying around you during the current flight; hover an aircraft to see its callsign, altitude and speed. When Taxiways is on in the tracking map, the log map also shows runways, taxiways and stands when you zoom in on the airport.
  • Each finished flight is kept: pick it in the list at the top to review it, or delete it. Flights are stored in the app's settings folder, not in the app folder.

All FSHub VAs (global radar)

The 🌍 ALL FSHUB VAS button adds the flights of all FSHub airlines, like the global radar on fshub.io: purple aircraft with a white outline (green in colour-blind mode), sized by category like AI traffic, showing, when you click the aircraft, the aircraft type, flight phase, altitude, speed and heading (no pilot names). Route and track of an FSHub flight

Click an aircraft from your VA or another FSHub VA: if the pilot filed a flight plan on FSHub, the route shows as white dashes with the waypoint names, and what has already been flown as a blue line. Clicking a line in your VA's list (bottom left) does the same: the map centres on the aircraft and shows its route and track.

Your track

A blue line follows your aircraft during the flight, like the "already flown" line of FSHub flights: compare at a glance the path actually flown with your SimBrief route. It is kept if you close the map, and starts again when you import a plan for another flight or your aircraft appears at another airport.

Automatic SimBrief plan

When the map opens, the plan you fetched in the SimBrief flight tab shows by itself, with a short green message. Two safeguards: if you did not fetch a plan in that tab (or the flight is over), the map stays blank; if your latest SimBrief plan is more than 12 hours old or is not the one in the tab, a message offers to import it anyway. The map's import button stays available.

Performance and runway wind

If your SimBrief plan was generated with the Runway Analysis option, the plan box adds one performance line, only for the useful phase: ▲ takeoff on the ground and in the climb (runway, V1, VR, V2, flaps, and in yellow the reduced-thrust temperature: SEL TEMP on Boeing, FLEX on Airbus), ▼ landing in the descent and approach (runway, VAPP, dry or wet runway), nothing in cruise. The landing part follows the arrival METAR live: wet runway when it rains, headwind, tailwind and crosswind on the planned runway, VAPP = VREF + half the headwind + gusts (between +5 and +20 kt), orange warning for tailwind or crosswind above your limit. The ▸ details button shows everything: runway lengths and landing distances in feet (actual, factored, margin), crosswind limit, ILS frequency and approach course of the planned runway, a Glideslope intercept altitude box: the altitude at which you capture the ILS glideslope, printed on your approach chart (e.g. 3000); type it once, it is kept for that airport and runway and shown in the short line (if SimBrief gives no ILS frequency, only the runway course is shown) and a ✈ SimBrief performance link to your latest plan for an exact calculation. Distances are those computed by SimBrief when the plan was created, not corrected for tailwind. Without SimBrief performance (light aircraft, no plan…), the box shows the wind on each runway of the useful airfield (departure on the ground, arrival in cruise and descent; without a plan, the nearest one), the advised runway and the density altitude. If the airfield publishes no METAR (small fields), the app takes the one from the nearest large or medium airport (up to 60 NM) and says so, e.g. “METAR from LFMT, 23 NM”; the departure and arrival METAR boxes do the same (“Nearest METAR: LFMT at 23 NM”).

Airport layouts (Taxiways button)

Zoom in on an airport (zoom 13 or more): the map draws the runways (dark grey, number in white), the taxiways (yellow centerline, letter in a black label), the aprons, the holding points (red) and the parking spots (turquoise, numbers shown when you zoom in further). Your aircraft and the traffic stay on top. These layouts come from OpenStreetMap (© OpenStreetMap contributors, ODbL license): they show the real airport, which may differ slightly from an add-on scenery.

  • The first time an airport is shown needs internet and a few seconds ("TAXIWAYS …" while loading). The layout is then kept on the PC and shows instantly, even offline. After 30 days, the app asks for it again to get the up-to-date airport; if the server does not answer at that moment, the old layout stays on screen: an airport already loaded never disappears.
  • Loaded in advance: as soon as your SimBrief plan is imported, the departure, arrival and alternate layouts load in the background. When you arrive, the taxiways show without waiting.
  • Some small airfields are barely or not drawn in OpenStreetMap: nothing shows then.
  • Labels: from afar, only the letters of the main taxiways show (A, B, Q…); zooming in shows all letters, then the parking numbers. The same letter is only repeated when it is far enough away, and labels never overlap.
  • TAXIWAYS ⚠: the OpenStreetMap server did not answer (often because it is overloaded). Hover the button to see why; the app tries again by itself 2 minutes later when you move the map.
  • Clicking Taxiways hides or shows the layouts again; your choice is kept.

The relay

The relay, built into Hangar FS 2024, links MSFS and the page: AI traffic, your aircraft's position, SimBrief, METAR, FSHub and airport layouts. It starts with the app and is controlled with the ⏻ button at the bottom of the menu; its status shows right next to it (active, waiting for MSFS, connected).

FMS (under construction)

The FMS menu button opens a small separate window to place in a corner of the screen during the flight. Load SimBrief fetches your latest plan; Open a .PLN loads a plan saved from the MSFS world map, the Flight plan / VFR plan pages or Little Navmap; Direct to… then a fix in the list picks the fix you fly to; New flight (press twice) clears the plan. Tap the cruise altitude at the top right, or a fix’s Alt. column, to type it: VNAV uses it (handy for a plan coming from the VFR plan page, which has no altitudes). Departure and arrival field elevations come from SimBrief, the .PLN or the airport database; if unknown, an orange “?” shows: tap it to type it. While the arrival elevation is unknown, VNAV does not descend below the last fix with an altitude. The Send to aircraft button prepares the FMS plan for the aircraft GPS, to see the route without the tablet: .PLN file for the MSFS 2024 tablet (default-aircraft G1000, G3000… only take a plan from the tablet: Route › Load / Save PLN File › Load from this PC › Plan FMS.pln › Send to avionics; the FMS keeps this file always up to date at every plan change and places it right in the folder where the tablet “Load from this PC” window opens (the MSFS 2024 folder), as well as in Documents › Hangar FS 2024: a double-click is enough; the “Open the folder” button shows the file), fpl.pln file of the PMS50 GTN (then Flight Plan › Import in the GTN) and .gfp file of the TDS GTN (then FPL › Menu › Catalog › Menu › Import). These GTN files are also rewritten automatically at every FMS plan change (for the TDS GTN, the file is then called HANGAR_FMS.gfp): you only have to import it in the GTN. Keep flying with the FMS LNAV / VNAV. The VFR plan page also sends its route to the FMS as soon as you change it (SID, STAR and approach included, with the ILS frequency): no need to copy it; the FMS then shows “last change: VFR plan”. A SimBrief plan imported in Flight tracking also goes to the FMS (if the FMS already had an approach for the same arrival airport, it is kept and joined to the end of the STAR); when the FMS has the route of the same flight, the map no longer shows the SimBrief route, so there is only one route. The Flight tracking map shows the FMS route (active leg in pink, passed fixes in grey, approach dashed), the planned altitude at each fix, the estimated ▲ T/C and the ▼ T/D, and a collapsible FMS box at the top right: next fix (distance, altitude), next altitude change (climb, T/D, VPATH descent) and ILS. The plan stays in memory: changing page, closing the window or restarting the app loses nothing. At the bottom, two buttons switch between the Flight plan and Autopilot screens. The latter commands your aircraft's autopilot: AP, HDG, NAV, APR, ALT, VS and SPD buttons, and heading, altitude, VS and speed targets with − and + (hold to go faster) or by tapping the value to type it. Under each button, “aircraft” means the aircraft handles that mode; “not handled” means it did not react. Aircraft with custom systems (Fenix, iFly…) may not respond. For a PMDG 737 or an iFly 737 MAX, the Autopilot screen becomes the aircraft MCP (read and commanded through the aircraft SDK: PMDG’s, or the “iFly Plugin” module shipped with the iFly), read and commanded through the PMDG SDK: CMD A and CMD B separately (or both), A/T, N1, SPEED, VNAV, LVL CHG, HDG SEL, LNAV, VOR/LOC, APP, ALT HLD, V/S, F/D (both together), and the IAS/Mach, heading, altitude, VS and course targets; the aircraft FMS keeps the route. The first time, the “Enable the PMDG SDK” button adds EnableDataBroadcast=1 to the aircraft options (a backup copy is kept): then reload the flight. The LNAV button makes the aircraft follow the app FMS route: the FMS computes the heading (wind included), sets it on the aircraft's HDG mode and moves to the next fix on its own; a Direct to… is followed at once. The NAV button makes the aircraft follow its own flight plan. Setting the heading by hand, turning HDG off or switching to NAV / APR disengages LNAV. Even without LNAV (aircraft FMS, NAV, hand flying), the flight plan list follows your position: each passed fix lights up green with a tick, and the next fix becomes the active one. The VNAV button manages altitude: climb to cruise altitude (VS +700), then the FMS computes the top of descent (TOD) to reach the planned altitudes at the fixes, warns “Descent in 1 min” (the ▼ T/D point also appears in place in the flight plan list, with the remaining distance when VNAV is engaged) and descends on a 3° path (VPATH) by setting the altitude target and VS; it stops when the aircraft captures the ILS glideslope. During the climb, changing VS with − / + just sets the climb VS, without disengaging anything; setting altitude, or VS during the descent, disengages VNAV. The Approach button (Flight plan screen) lists the destination approaches (ILS, LOC, RNAV…, from the MSFS navigation data imported from the VFR plan page); pick the approach then the entry point (or “Vectors”), and its fixes are added to the route. The runway threshold (RW…) never has a target altitude; each approach fix gets the altitude from the MSFS data (“A” = at or above, “B” = at or below), and the final approach fix is marked FAF; if the data was imported before this version, import again (VFR plan › Update from MSFS), otherwise the FAF gets 3000 ft by default (field + 1500 ft if higher), marked with a “*”: tap the altitude to correct it from the chart (the “*” points just before take the same altitude). VNAV descends to that altitude, then the ILS takes over. For an ILS, the FMS finds its frequency and course: Auto ILS puts the frequency in NAV1 standby around 80 NM, swaps it at 25 NM, sets the course, arms LOC first (NAV mode) around 18 NM, then APR once the localizer is captured; VNAV stops at glideslope capture. At the bottom of the Autopilot screen, two independent buttons: Auto / Manual radios (frequency and course) and Auto / Manual LOC/APP (arming LOC then APP). All four combinations work; with manual radios and auto LOC/APP, arming happens as soon as the right frequency is active. On the PMDG 737 and iFly 737 MAX, auto radios tune NAV1 and NAV2 and both MCP courses (left and right), and auto LOC/APP presses the MCP VOR/LOC then APP (only when CMD A or CMD B is engaged). Airbus A220 (Synaptic / iniBuilds): the Autopilot screen shows an FCP panel (AP, A/T, left and right F/D together, HDG, NAV, APPR, FLC, ALT, VS, VNAV) with heading, altitude, VS and speed; for altitude, VS and speed, the FMS turns the aircraft knob step by step up to the wanted value (a few seconds). The A220 FMC tunes the ILS itself: the FMS Auto ILS leaves it alone. Auto COM (button at the bottom of the Autopilot screen, off by default to let SayIntentions or your ATC do it): the FMS reads your departure and arrival airport frequencies from MSFS and tunes COM1 at each phase, the frequency to use as active and the next one in standby (you just swap). Parked: ATIS then delivery / ground; taxi: ground then tower; takeoff: tower then departure; climb: departure; 80 NM from arrival: ATIS in standby; 40 NM: approach then tower; final: tower then ground; after landing: ground. The change happens only once per phase: if you tune something else by hand, the FMS leaves it. Charts (3rd button at the bottom of the FMS window): a diagram of the departure (SID) or arrival (STAR and approach) drawn from your flight plan, with fixes, altitude constraints (≥ at or above, ≤ at or below), the FAF, 10, 20 and 30 NM rings around the airport, your aircraft and the active leg in magenta; it is for orientation, not a navigation chart. For a French airport, the Official chart (SIA) button opens the airport page of the SIA eAIP (current AIRAC cycle) in your browser, with all its official charts (SID, STAR, IAC). The Navigraph button (for subscribers) copies the airport code and opens Navigraph Charts in your browser: paste the code (Ctrl+V) into its search. Navigraph does not allow opening a specific chart from another app.

Administrator mode, plainly

  • The "Always open in administrator mode" tile is useful for apps that require administrator rights (SayIntentions, REX Atmos…). It makes the app run as administrator without Windows confirmation every time it opens (double-click, shortcut, or PC startup if the "Start with Windows" tile is on). Both tiles are independent: administrator mode does not make the app start with Windows. To do so, the app starts normally (startup shortcut), then restarts itself through an "on demand" scheduled task that never starts anything by itself. Some antivirus software may still flag this mode: only switch it on if you need it.
  • "Current mode" tells how the app runs now. If restarting as administrator fails (antivirus, non-administrator account, old task), the app says so clearly. If you moved the .exe, it offers to update the task (one confirmation).
  • Restart now as administrator switches to administrator mode right away (one Windows confirmation).
  • This mode lets you launch, without confirmation, the apps that require it, and move them to your 2nd screen.

Screens

  1. The diagram shows your screens; the chosen one is blue, MSFS stays on the primary screen.
  2. Window screen: "Automatic" sends the windows to the 2nd screen if connected, or choose a specific screen.
  3. Identify screens shows a big number on each screen for 3 seconds.
  4. Switch on the tiles of the windows to place: Hangar FS 2024, Scenery map, Flight plan & tracking (full screen).

With a single screen, or if the chosen screen is disconnected, everything opens on the primary screen. A window already open stays where you put it.

My FSHub VA

  1. Your VA code: type your airline's code, the one in its fshub.io address (for example LFV for fshub.io/airline/LFV), then Enter. Its pilots in flight show on the tracking map, without a key.
  2. FSHub key (optional): it only recognises your own aircraft, so it is not shown twice. On fshub.io, click your name at the top right, then Settings → Integrations, and generate your personal key. Paste it in the field (it shows as dots; Show to check it).
  3. Click Test the key: you should read for example "✓ YourName · Les Fous Volants (LFV) · 4 pilots online".

Without a VA code, your key is enough: the app uses the airline of your FSHub profile. Without code or key, nothing is shown and the ★ MY FSHUB VA button stays greyed out.

The key stays on your PC and only the relay uses it. Never share it, and hide it before taking a screenshot. If it was seen, regenerate it on FSHub and paste the new one.
